title: Adab with the earth
hook: the end of the world arrives, and there's a seedling in your hand

segments.voice: Yesterday, adab with creation, and your line: every creature counts. Did an animal get water or food from you? Today, the ground they all stand on. Day one thousand three hundred five.

The Hour has come. The end of everything. And there you are, holding a small palm shoot, roots still in a clump of soil. What now? The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, answered that exact question. In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, in paraphrase: if the Hour is established and one of you has a seedling in his hand, and he is able to plant it before he stands up, let him plant it. Today: the manners owed to the earth itself.
screen: `THE HOUR HAS COME.` → `A SEEDLING IN YOUR HAND.` → `PLANT IT.`

segments.voice: Sit with how strange that is. If the world is ending, nobody will eat the dates. Nobody will rest in the shade. And still: plant it. The hadith pulls the act loose from its result. Planting isn't only for the harvest. It's what a person on the earth does. Then the Qur'an gives the reason the earth is in our hands at all. Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." Khalifa. A deputy, a steward, someone looking after what belongs to another. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet adds: the world is sweet and green, and Allah has made you successors in it, to see how you act. Stewards are watched for how they treat the estate. Then a hadith that turns the garden into worship. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: whenever a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, or a person, or an animal eats from it, it counts as charity for him. By that hadith, even the sparrow that steals your figs leaves a charity behind. So the adab with the earth comes down to three movements. Plant, even when you won't see the fruit. Look after it as a steward, not an owner. And let the birds have their share. This closes the stretch on the manners of daily life, down to the soil underfoot. Tomorrow the path turns inward, to the virtues.
screen: `PLANT IT, EVEN AT THE END.` · `A VICEROY IN THE EARTH.` · `SWEET AND GREEN, AND WATCHED.` · `THE BIRD'S SHARE IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Feel your weight resting on the ground, or on a floor built on the ground. Bring to mind one small patch of earth you can reach: a pot on the windowsill, a yard, a planter by the door, a crack in the sidewalk where something is already trying. Picture putting something into it. A seed, a cutting, a bulb, or just water for a plant that's thirsty. Notice you don't need to see it grow. If you pray, you can offer that small planting with the remembrance of Allah. The bell holds the time.
Adab with the earth. The manners of a steward: planting even when you won't see the fruit, looking after what was entrusted, and letting the birds have their share. Today's word.
Your line: plant it anyway. Today, put one thing in the ground or in a pot, or water something that's growing. Tomorrow, humility that raises. Day one thousand three hundred five.

howItsDone: Islamic teaching on the earth draws on the Qur'an's description of humanity as khalifa, a steward on the earth, and on hadith that count planting as charity and that urge planting a seedling even when the Hour comes.
